Witness: A 5-cycle or a graph where two vertices on level 2 are connected by an edge but have different parents on level 1 (e.g. C5: s-u-b-c-v-s with no chords) has a cross edge (b, c) at level 2, which does not form a triangle. BFS scanning the adjacency list of b cannot distinguish in O(1) time whether b and c share a common neighbor on level 1 without checking, and if they do not share a parent, edge (b, c) does not even lie in a triangle with their BFS tree parents; conversely, even if both are children of a, if b and c were already discovered by a, scanning (b, c) requires verifying their common parent, but when other level 1 vertices exist, cross edges at level 2 form 4- or 5-cycles rather than triangles, so BFS in O(m) cannot reliably detect a triangle this way without false positives or extra checks that take super-linear time per search unless matrix multiplication is used, which invalidates the claim that BFS+(s) detects a triangle in O(m) time as described in Case 2.1.

Some intuition. The idea behind the algorithm is to get in a position to be able to detect a 
triangle during a Breadth First Search (BFS) from a suitable vertex. Specifically we will use the 
following slightly modified version of BFS with a start vertex s. For a standard version, the reader 
can refer for instance to [27, Ch. 7].

findings.explanation: high confidence.  Witness: Counterexample to the case analysis: let G have a triangle T = {a, b, c} and an additional vertex u connected to s and b (but not to a or c). In Case 2.1, when s is sampled, both u and a are at level 1. If u is scanned before a, b is discovered as a child of u (parent(b) = u), whereas c is discovered as a child of a (parent(c) = a). When edge (b, c) between level 2 vertices is encountered, neither {u, b, c} nor {a, b, c} is immediately identified as a triangle during standard BFS edge examination without extra adjacency checks, violating the claim that BFS⁺ correctly detects a triangle in all such configurations in O(m) time per sample without additional overhead that would break the runtime bound or correctness proof across BFS levels in Case 2.1/2.2. Therefore, the case analysis is flawed and Theorem 2 does not hold as stated with the claimed guarantees and runtime bounds based on this analysis alone; the reduction and subcubic combinatorial bound are unproven in this manner given the false premise in Case 2.1 and Case 2.2 regarding BFS levels and parents of cross-edges in general graphs without triangle detection or listing every 2-path across levels, which would take much longer than O(m) per BFS trial in dense graphs or when many cross edges exist between levels with different parents. Hence the claimed algorithm and bound in Theorem 2 are false/unsubstantiated by the proof given in the paper. The correct status of subcubic combinatorial triangle detection remains open, and the claimed O(n^{7/3}) combinatorial bound does not follow from the provided BFS⁺ procedure and case breakdown because a cross edge between two vertices on level 2 does not imply a triangle with either vertex's BFS parent when their parents differ or when the common neighbor is not tracked correctly within O(m) total time per search tree traversal without extra matrix lookups for all cross edges which would exceed the claimed O(m) BFS runtime bound in graphs with up to Omega(m) cross edges and high degrees. Thus Theorem 2 is incorrect as proven in the paper. (Note: Itai-Rodeh and related results show that combinatorial triangle detection remains open at subcubic exponents O(n^{3-\epsilon})). evidence.text:
Theorem 2. There is a randomized algorithm for triangle detection in a given n-vertex graph with 
m edges running in O(m^(2/3)n) = O(n^(7/3)) time, and whose probability of error is at most 10^(−30). 
Alternatively, this task can be handled in O(mn^(1/2)) time, or in O(m^(4/3)) time.
